problem:
Meridian Bank operates in several countries from a single payment engine, and a rejected payment must be explained to the customer. The internal diagnostic reason for a rejection is often precise and sensitive: it may state that the beneficiary account is closed, that the account holder name does not match, or that the account is subject to a restriction. In some jurisdictions, disclosing that detail to the payer would reveal private information about the beneficiary, which local privacy rules forbid. In others, the customer is entitled to a fuller explanation. The bank's current configuration applies one reason text everywhere, so it either discloses too much in a restricted jurisdiction or gives a vague, unhelpful message where a fuller explanation is permitted.

The problem surfaced when a corporate customer in a restricted jurisdiction received a rejection notice that stated the beneficiary account was closed, and the beneficiary complained that their account status had been disclosed to a third party. Compliance opened a review, and the product team discovered that the reason-code mapping had no country dimension at all: one internal code mapped to one external text for every entity and every country. Operations also reported the opposite failure, where customers in other jurisdictions received only a generic code and opened support cases because they could not tell whether to correct the account number, contact the beneficiary, or simply retry.

The bank needs a design that keeps full diagnostic detail for Operations and audit, while disclosing only what each jurisdiction permits to each audience. The configuration must be explicit about its scope, engine, country or entity, so a change for one country cannot silently change the message a customer sees in another.
solution:
Separate the reason into three layers and never let them collapse into one field. The internal diagnostic reason stays in the payment record and the Operations view, with the full detail needed to investigate. The customer-visible reason is derived from it through a governed mapping table that is keyed by internal code, country, entity and channel, and that produces only the approved external text for that jurisdiction. The scheme reason code sent to the counterparty follows the scheme's own code list, so the external message the counterparty sees is a scheme code, not the bank's internal wording.

Govern the mapping as configuration, not as code buried in the engine. Each mapping row needs an owner, an effective date, a privacy review sign-off and a language version, because the same code may need different wording in different languages and the permitted wording can change when local rules change. Changes go through a controlled release with regression tests that run the same rejection through every country and entity configuration and assert the exact customer-visible text for each, so a change for one country cannot silently alter another.

Finally, make the audit trail prove what was disclosed and to whom. Log the internal code, the mapped external text, the jurisdiction applied and the channel for every rejection notice, so Compliance can evidence that a restricted disclosure never happened. Provide Operations with a separate diagnostic view that shows the internal reason without exposing it to the customer, and give the support team a scripted explanation for each external code so customers get consistent, permitted help when they call.

decision.question: You are the business analyst for Meridian Bank's payment engine. A rejection reason contains sensitive beneficiary account information. In one operating country, local privacy rules forbid disclosing it to the payer; in another, a fuller explanation is permitted. Compliance asks you to recommend the design.

options.label: A
options.detail: Remove reason codes entirely and tell customers only that the payment failed.

options.label: B
options.detail: Use one generic reason text for every country so nothing sensitive is ever disclosed anywhere.

options.label: C
options.detail: Disclose the full internal reason to every customer so Operations receives fewer support calls.

options.label: D
options.detail: Keep internal diagnostic detail separate from customer-visible text, and apply jurisdiction-specific disclosure rules with a governed reason-code catalogue mapped to scheme codes.

decisionRationale: Option D is correct because it preserves operational transparency internally while disclosing only what each jurisdiction permits externally, with a governed catalogue so the mapping is controlled and testable. Option B is safe but unhelpful, and it drives support calls where a fuller explanation is allowed. Option C breaches privacy rules in restricted jurisdictions. Option A leaves customers unable to correct the problem and leaves Operations without a usable reason.

happy: A payment is rejected for a sensitive reason. Operations sees the full diagnostic detail and can act on it. The counterparty receives the correct scheme code. The customer receives an accurate explanation that is permitted in their jurisdiction, in their language, with enough guidance to correct the problem or contact the beneficiary. The audit record proves exactly what was disclosed.

negative.title: Internal reason accidentally exposed
negative.detail: A mapping row is missing for a country, and the system falls back to the internal text. Default to the most restrictive approved text when no mapping exists, alert Compliance and Operations, and block the notification until a governed mapping is added.

negative.title: Unknown reason code
negative.detail: A new scheme or engine code has no entry in the catalogue. Route the payment to an Operations queue with the raw code, apply the generic permitted text to the customer, and add the code to the catalogue through the governed change process.

negative.title: Language mismatch
negative.detail: The customer language has no approved translation for the external text. Fall back to the approved text in the default language for that jurisdiction, log the gap, and commission the translation through the governed process rather than machine-translating a sensitive message on the fly.

negative.title: Mapping change affects another country
negative.detail: A change intended for one jurisdiction alters the text shown in another. Run the full country and entity regression suite before release, assert the exact text per jurisdiction, and roll back the mapping change if any assertion fails.

technical: Model the reason as three separate attributes: internal diagnostic code, scheme code, and customer-visible text key. Never store the internal wording in the same field as the customer text, and never let a channel read the internal field directly. Key the mapping by internal code, country, entity, channel and language, with effective-from and effective-to dates so a rule change can be staged and audited. Version the catalogue and keep prior versions for historical reconstruction of what a customer was told. Use correlation IDs to link the rejection, the mapping applied, the notification sent and the audit record. Test the mapping matrix exhaustively across country and entity combinations in the regression suite, including the missing-mapping fallback.

accounting: A rejected payment must not leave a dangling accounting entry, so any reservation or debit raised when the payment was accepted is reversed once, and the reversal is linked to the original instruction reference. Operations works from a rejection worklist that shows the internal diagnostic reason, the external text sent, the jurisdiction applied and the age of the item, with SLA targets for customer follow-up where the customer must correct and resubmit. Support teams use the governed explanation script for each external code, and Compliance reviews a sample of disclosures each month against the jurisdiction rules. A privacy breach caused by an incorrect disclosure is treated as an incident with notification to Compliance and a mapping fix through the governed change process.
